mcqs.question: What does a difference array's entry diff[i] represent, for i > 0?
options: The sum of all elements from 0 to i
The change from arr[i-1] to arr[i]
The maximum value in arr up to index i
The original value of arr[i] unchanged
mcqs.explanation: diff[i] = arr[i] - arr[i-1] records the delta between consecutive elements, which is why it's zero wherever a run of equal values continues. It's the inverse of a prefix sum, which accumulates rather than records deltas — it isn't a running sum, a running max, or a copy of the original value.

mcqs.question: To add v to every element in arr[l..r], a difference array update sets diff[l] += v and diff[r+1] -= v. Why does the -v at r+1 matter?
options: It's a rounding correction needed only for floating-point values
It cancels the +v exactly one position past r, so the increment stops affecting the array beyond the intended range
It converts the update from an addition to a subtraction
It's optional — omitting it only affects performance, not correctness
mcqs.explanation: The -v cancels the running total exactly past r during reconstruction, keeping the increment scoped to [l, r]. Omitting it is a correctness bug, not a performance one, since the +v would otherwise propagate to every later index once the prefix-sum pass runs.

mcqs.question: Applying k range-increment updates to an array of size n with a difference array, then reconstructing the final array, costs how much in total?
options: O(n · k), same as applying each update directly
O(k log n), from a balanced tree of updates
O(n + k) — O(k) for the point writes plus O(n) for one reconstruction pass
O(n) regardless of k, since updates are free
mcqs.explanation: Each update costs O(1) as two point writes, so k updates cost O(k); the single prefix-sum reconstruction at the end costs O(n) regardless of k — giving O(n + k) total, far better than the O(n·k) worst case of applying each update by looping over its range.

mcqs.question: When does the naive per-update loop (adding v to every element in [l, r] directly) perform worst compared to a difference array?
options: The naive loop and the difference array always perform identically
When there is only a single update covering the whole array
When updates are applied to a sorted array
When there are many updates and each spans a large fraction of the array
mcqs.explanation: The naive loop's cost scales with the range width times the number of updates, so many wide-range updates push it toward O(n·k); the difference array's cost is O(1) per update regardless of range width. A single update over the whole array is just one O(n) pass either way — the gap only widens as k grows, and sortedness is irrelevant.

mcqs.question: A range update applies diff[l] += v but the developer forgets diff[r+1] -= v. What's the observable effect?
options: The program crashes immediately with an index error
Nothing — the missing subtraction only matters if r equals n-1
The increment v silently applies to every index from l through the end of the array, not just up to r
The update is simply ignored and has no effect at all
mcqs.explanation: Without the cancellation, the prefix-sum reconstruction keeps carrying +v forward past r all the way to the end of the array, so the update leaks beyond its intended range rather than crashing or vanishing. This happens regardless of whether r is the last index — the missing pair is required for every update.

mcqs.question: A system needs the true current value of an array index immediately after every single range update, not just at the end. Is a difference array the right structure?
options: Yes, difference arrays support O(1) reads after every update by design
No — values aren't materialized until the prefix-sum reconstruction runs, so per-update reads need a different structure like a Fenwick or segment tree
Yes, as long as the array is resized to n+1 first
No — difference arrays only support a single update total, never a batch
mcqs.explanation: A difference array defers all real values until one reconstruction pass at the end, so it only pays off when updates are batched before any read — interleaved reads need a structure built for that, like a Fenwick tree or segment tree with range-update support. Resizing to n+1 only fixes the boundary write, and difference arrays are explicitly meant for batches of updates, not just one.
